summary: Defines the Internationalized Resource Identifier (IRI), a complement to the URI built from characters in the Unicode universal character set. It defines a mapping from IRIs to URIs, so IRIs can be used where URIs are required.

plainLanguage.summary: An Internationalized Resource Identifier (IRI) lets people write a resource address with characters from many writing systems. When a system only accepts a URI, software converts the IRI using a defined UTF-8 and percent-encoding process.

questions: how to convert an iri to a uri
subtitle: A resource identifier that can be written in characters from the Unicode character set.

tldr.problem: URI syntax uses a limited subset of US-ASCII, which makes identifiers harder to write in many languages.
tldr.mechanism: An IRI extends URI syntax with selected Unicode characters. Software maps non-ASCII characters to UTF-8 octets and percent-encodes those octets when a URI is required.
tldr.outcome: IRIs can identify resources in formats that accept them. A URI-only protocol still needs the defined mapping.

today: RFC 3987 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why IRIs Are Needed
sections.content:
A URI uses a limited subset of US-ASCII characters. People often use identifiers as words, so relying on Latin letters can make them harder to remember and enter in languages that use other scripts.

RFC 3987 defines an Internationalized Resource Identifier (IRI) as a sequence of Unicode characters. It keeps IRIs distinct from URIs so existing software that accepts only URIs is not silently changed.
sections.plainLanguage: IRIs let people write resource addresses with characters from their own languages. The separate IRI name keeps older URI-only systems clear about what they can accept.

sections.title: Characters and IRI Syntax
sections.content:
An IRI is a sequence of characters, not bytes. Its syntax follows URI syntax, with permitted Universal Character Set characters beyond U+007F added to the unreserved set. Private-use characters may appear only in the query component.

URI components and reserved characters keep their usual roles. Characters outside US-ASCII are not delimiters, and this syntax does not support IPv6 scoped addressing zone identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: An IRI follows the same structure as a URI, but some components can contain additional Unicode characters. These added characters do not replace punctuation that separates parts of an address.

sections.title: Converting an IRI to a URI
sections.content:
Applications must map IRIs to URIs in two steps. First, they produce a Unicode character sequence; input from a non-Unicode encoding is normalized to NFC, while Unicode-encoded input is not normalized. Second, each permitted non-ASCII character is encoded as UTF-8 and each resulting octet is written as a percent-encoding.

Hexadecimal letters in percent-encodings should be uppercase. Existing percent-encoded sequences and characters already allowed in URIs are not encoded again. For domain names, an implementation may use the ToASCII operation when the scheme permits that approach.
sections.plainLanguage: To make an IRI usable by a URI-only system, software encodes each permitted non-ASCII character as UTF-8 and writes its bytes with percent signs. It should not encode characters a second time when they already have a valid URI form.

sections.title: Converting a URI Back to an IRI
sections.content:
Converting a URI to an IRI is optional. The procedure decodes percent-encoded octets only when they form legal UTF-8 and the resulting character is permitted in an IRI; reserved characters and percent signs remain encoded.

Implementations must not guess a different character encoding from context. A URI containing percent-encoded bytes from another encoding could map back to a different URI if those bytes were guessed as Unicode characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Software can show Unicode characters in place of some percent-encoded bytes. It must use UTF-8 only, because guessing another encoding can change the address.

sections.title: Comparing and Normalizing IRIs
sections.content:
IRI comparison estimates whether two identifiers are equivalent; it cannot prove that they identify different resources. The RFC describes a comparison ladder: simple character comparison, syntax-based normalization, scheme-based normalization, and protocol-based normalization.

Higher steps can reduce false negatives but require more processing. Comparison must use characters in a common encoding. Applications using IRIs as identity tokens must use simple string comparison, and comparison-only normalization must not alter the original IRI passed onward.
sections.plainLanguage: Software can compare addresses exactly or apply additional rules, such as case rules defined by a scheme. More rules may recognize more equivalent addresses, but the original address should be preserved when it is sent elsewhere.

sections.title: Security and Display Risks
sections.content:
Incorrect encoding or decoding can cause a character such as a slash to be interpreted differently after a security check. Some UTF-8 decoders accept overlong byte sequences, which can make an encoded path separator bypass checks.

IRIs can also be spoofed with characters that look alike, inconsistent normalization, multiple accepted encodings, or bidirectional text that displays differently from its logical order. Correct Unicode bidirectional processing and careful handling of look-alike characters are important.
sections.plainLanguage: Different characters can look alike, and faulty decoding can change how an address is interpreted. Software must handle Unicode and encoding consistently so a misleading address does not pass a check.
